newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia aluminium's poor image threatens investment.
newsitem.headline: Russia aluminium's poor image threatens investment.

text.p: Russia's key aluminium sector has a serious image problem which threatens to scare off the foreign investors it needs to flourish in the post-Soviet era, senior metal traders said on Wednesday.

From protectionist trade rhetoric to criminal investigations, the sector could end up shooting itself in the foot if it and the government fail to present a more attractive face to the West, they said.
Russia has enjoyed some success in wooing overseas partners to its aluminium sector, where their participation has helped it rise to number one in the world export rankings.
But Moscow is mulling new duties on raw material imports that would help domestic producers of alumina, the main raw material used to make aluminium, but penalise foreign partners.

"Obviously a hike in import duties would affect our operations here," said David Reuben, chairman of London-based Trans-World Group. "These plants need urgent investment and finances have to be found," he told Reuters by telephone.
Trading firms like Trans-World and Swiss-based Glencore AG import alumina into Russia, pay aluminium smelters to process it and have the right to export finished metal on to world markets.
They do not pay import duties under the current system.

The deals, known as tolling, account for 60-70 percent of Russia's aluminium output. Russia produced last year 2.87 million tonnes of the metal, used in applications ranging from drinking cans to car parts, and exported 2.44 million.

Trans-World alone markets around one million tonnes of Russian aluminium annually, although it only owns about a third of this. It operates at Bratsk, the world's biggest smelter located in Siberia, and at Sayansk, Russia's third biggest.

Russia does not produce enough alumina to feed its plants, and Reuben said any penalty on western partners' operations would hit aluminium production and exports. At today's prices, annual aluminium exports are worth over $4 billion.
"The most damaging thing is that the less alumina is brought in, the less aluminium gets produced and the less jobs there are. It's simple economics," Reuben said.
Another problem for trading companies wanting to work in Russia is the aluminium industry's image as a sector where crime is rife.
Banks may be put off financing trading operations or costly plant upgrades by the industry's poor image at home and abroad, which is not always justified, Reuben said.
"People say there is crime in aluminium. There may be crime at some plants, but why bring all of them into it because of the misdeeds of one plant in one area?" he said.
"This does not help the aluminium industry. How do you approach a bank which has heard of this kind of thing?"

Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov is locked in a battle against what he has called the "crime-ridden" world of Russian aluminium. Tussles for control of major plants can also dent confidence in the industry, traders said.
Russian media most recently focused on leadership changes at the Krasnoyarsk aluminium plant.
Igor Vishnyevsky, a Glencore employee, was dropped by the board from his post of general director of the Siberian smelter on Tuesday after only two weeks in the job.
He replaced Igor Kolpakov, who resigned after the Interior Ministry said it was investigating allegations that he mishandled funds. Kolpakov says he has done nothing wrong and can clear his name.
The changes in leadership and infighting at the plant, which is Russia and the world's second largest after Bratsk, are damaging the sector, Vishnyevsky said.
"I am quite sure this fighting is harmful for the aluminium sector in general," he said.

He said he hoped Krasnoyarsk would honour its contracts with Glencore this year, which account for 300,000 tonnes of total annual output at the smelter of around 780,000 tonnes. But beyond that the outlook was unclear.
